header: Date: 2026-08-26 | Start: 15:00 PDT | Duration: 47m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (ArborWave Head of Platform), Samir Khan (Network Eng), Priya Rao (Security)
summary: Discovery focused on ArborWave's private/VPC onramp constraints and customer-managed KMS requirements. Main risks: egress IP pinning, region data residency (eu-west-1 preference), and BYOK HSM integration. Agreed next steps: send security pack, schedule SE deep dive, and customer to share network details.
topics: Transit Gateway vs PrivateLink / interface endpoints
Region and data residency constraints (primary eu-west-1)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we have about 45 minutes. Quick intros?
[00:12] Lena (ArborWave): Hi, I'm Lena, Head of Platform, we've been exploring LLM inference options — main priorities are data residency, and we need to keep inference traffic inside eu-west-1.
[00:28] Maya: Great, that's helpful. Jordan and I will help map how Redwood Private can fit into your VPC topology — Jordan is our SE.
[00:35] Jordan (Redwood SE): Hey all. Quick note: we support Transit Gateway peering, VPC peering, and AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints). Each has different tradeoffs around cross-account routing and egress.
[00:50] Samir (ArborWave): Our primary constraint is we cannot punch a public egress for inference; outbound traffic has to go through our NATs and egress IPs are whitelisted by the PCI team.
[01:05] Priya (Security): Also we require customer-managed keys for any persisted artifacts, and FIPS certification for key usage — can you support BYOK / HSM?
[01:18] Jordan: Yes, we have options. For Redwood Private we support customer-managed KMS where the customer holds the CMK in their account and we use a cross-account role with key policy to encrypt stored artifacts. For HSM, we have a YubiHSM integration path and can discuss HSM-wrapped keys — there's an extra compliance review.
[01:36] Lena: When you say \"use\" the CMK, is Redwood service-side encryption using our key or will data leave our control?
[01:45] Jordan: Good question. The flow we usually follow is: you create a CMK, allow Redwood's service principal in the key policy for encrypt/decrypt, we never export plaintext keys — Redwood requests decrypt via the KMS API in your account. If you prefer HSM-only operations we can limit operations to wrapped keys and integrate via a customer HSM bridging setup, but that adds ops complexity.
[02:10] Samir: That sounds promising. On network layer, we prefer PrivateLink to avoid route table changes — do you recommend PrivateLink or Transit Gateway?
[02:22] Jordan: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) is clean for cross-account access and doesn't require route table propagation. But throughput and per-ENI scaling can be a constraint for high qps workloads. Transit Gateway or VPC peering gives higher throughput and simpler internal routing but requires cross-account peering and route table adjustments. For high throughput low-latency workloads, customers often choose dedicated VPC peering + shared services routing.
[02:45] Priya: If we go with PrivateLink, how do you manage egress — like our responses may need to reference internal resources, or we want to ensure everything egresses through our firewall?
[02:57] Jordan: With PrivateLink, traffic stays within AWS network and you can apply security controls on your side. If Redwood needs to access external model artifacts, we can place model cache in your VPC (in Private deployment) so nothing goes to public internet. For egress IPs specifically, if Redwood needs to call back into your systems, we can provide static outbound IP ranges from our side when on Dedicated, but for Private (customer VPC) calls originate from inside your VPC so they use your NATs — that should satisfy allowlist requirements.
[03:28] Maya: Quick clarification: when we say Dedicated vs Private — Dedicated is Redwood-managed GPUs in our cloud account but with isolated pools; Private is deployed into your VPC or VPC peered environment. Correct?
[03:38] Jordan: Exactly. Dedicated = Redwood-managed capacity but our infrastructure. Private = runtime inside your VPC, or endpoints connected into your account so you control networking and keys.
[03:48] Lena: Our compliance folks will push for Private because they want audit logs and network egress under our control.
[03:55] Maya: Totally understood. We also have audit log integrations (CloudTrail forwarding or a syslog sink) — we can include details in the security pack.
[04:05] Samir: For VPC design, we have limited /16 split across teams; we need guidance on subnet sizing for the inference nodes, ENIs, and interface endpoints. Do you have recommendations?
[04:18] Jordan: Yes, we'll share a sizing guide. Quick rule of thumb: for interface endpoints you need one ENI per AZ and scaling for throughput; for peering/transit gateway you need room for additional route table entries. We'll include a sample overlay with recommended /22 blocks per AZ for node pools.
[04:35] Priya: Any specifics around KMS key policy? We want to ensure Redwood cannot create new keys in our account.
[04:42] Jordan: Your key policy can restrict CreateKey to your admins. For usage we ask you to add our service principal with Encrypt/Decrypt/IAM policy for that CMK. We can provide the exact policy snippet.
[04:56] Lena: Latency: our product needs p95 < 120ms for short prompt calls. Do you have guidance on latency for eu-west-1 if we host Private vs Dedicated?
[05:07] Jordan: If you run Private in eu-west-1 inside your VPC, network latency is minimal — the biggest factor is model size and batching. For small models p95 can be sub-100ms; for large Llama 2-variants it's higher. Our Optimize team can suggest quantization and batching settings to meet p95 targets while controlling cost.
[05:28] Samir: Bandwidth cost is a concern — large models generate a lot of token traffic. If responses are 2k tokens for some diagnostic logs, that's heavy. Is there server-side compression or streaming?
[05:40] Maya: We support streaming and token-level batching to reduce egress. Also prefix caching can help for repeated contexts. We'll include common patterns in the runbook.
[05:50] Priya: About auditability — we need immutable logs for each inference call for 90 days. Can we ingest those into our Splunk/CloudWatch?
[05:59] Jordan: Yes. We can forward call-level metadata (no PII or model outputs unless you opt-in) into your logging destination. For full outputs we recommend storing them in your S3 bucket encrypted with your CMK.
[06:18] Lena: Good. For the onboarding timeline: we want a pilot in eu-west-1 within 6 weeks. Is that feasible?
[06:26] Maya: Yes, typical pilot timeline is 4–8 weeks depending on your networking approvals and KMS approvals. The gating items will be: (1) provisioning the peering/PrivateLink, (2) KMS policy signoff, (3) egress allowlist if any, and (4) test dataset for quality checks.
[06:43] Samir: One practical: we use a Transit Gateway and cross-account routes for other vendors. Would Redwood require a dedicated TGW attachment, or can we use an existing TGW?
[06:56] Jordan: You can use your existing TGW. We'll ask for the TGW attachment details and route domain. Sometimes customers prefer a dedicated attachment for easier isolation, but it's not mandatory. We'll document both flows.
[07:12] Priya: Do you support SAML/SSO to administer the private deployment? We want RBAC mapped to our IdP.
[07:20] Maya: Yes, we support SSO (SAML 2.0 / OIDC) and RBAC mapping. For Private deployments we can federate admin roles into your IdP and sync groups. We'll include the SSO onboarding notes.
[07:34] Lena: For compliance signoff, our legal will want to see data flow diagrams and the SLA for Private — can you send those?
[07:42] Maya: Absolutely. We'll include the Private SLA, dataflow, and example diagrams in the security pack.
[07:50] Samir: One more - IP addressing: if we peer, will you require non-overlapping CIDRs?
[07:56] Jordan: Yes, peering requires non-overlapping CIDRs. For TGW you can have overlapping on some providers but it's messy; best to provide your CIDR plan and we can advise a clean carve-out.
[08:08] Lena: Hypothetical: if we go Dedicated to start faster, but later migrate to Private, how painless is that?
[08:17] Jordan: We support staged migration. Dedicated is a quicker path: you get reserved capacity in our environment with static egress IPs for allowlisting. Later we can export model state / weights and switch traffic to Private with a canary rollout. We'll outline what artifacts are needed for migration.
[08:33] Priya: Any SOC2 / ISO artifacts you can share now?
[08:37] Maya: We'll attach our SOC 2 type II report summary and ISO scope doc. Full attestations we can share under an NDA if required.
[08:46] Samir: On certs and mutual TLS — do you support mTLS between our services and the inference endpoints?
[08:52] Jordan: Yes, when using PrivateLink or peering we can enable mTLS for API calls to the runtime. For Private deployments we can also put a gateway in front with client cert verification. We'll document certificate rotation as well.
[09:05] Lena: Good. Let's talk about the small details: subnets, route tables, security group rules required.
[09:12] Jordan: For peered deployment, security groups should allow inbound from your app subnets to the inference node ports (we'll list ports in the doc). For PrivateLink, you'll create interface endpoints in each AZ and attach SGs there. We will provide a template Terraform and CloudFormation snippet.
[09:34] Priya: About data residency: we have a regulatory requirement that logs that contain user PII must not leave region. If you store any outputs in S3, it must be in eu-west-1 under our bucket.
[09:46] Jordan: That's supported; we can configure storage to be in your account and region and encrypted with your CMK.
[09:52] Maya: Action summary: we'll send security pack with sample policies, network diagram, and KMS policy snippet. Jordan will run the technical deep dive and we expect ArborWave to provide CIDR and NAT details.
[10:03] Lena: Sounds good. Anything else?
[10:06] Samir: Not now. We'll pull the subnet/cidr details.
[10:09] Priya: I'll review the KMS snippet and flag anything FIPS related.
[10:13] Maya: Great. We'll follow up in email with links to docs: security pack (https://redwood.example.com/security/arborwave), VPC checklist (https://redwood.example.com/onramp/vpc-checklist), and private KMS runbook (link in pack).
[10:26] Lena: Thanks everyone.
[10:29] Maya: Thanks, talk soon.
[10:32] [meeting ends — recording stops]
